prime.problem: Prefix sums on changing data force a bad choice: a plain array makes each query sum up to n numbers, and a prefix-sum array makes each update rewrite up to n prefixes. At n = 10⁶ either side costs 10⁶ steps.
prime.fits: Second in Trees and heaps. It is a tree with no pointers at all: an array whose index bits say what each cell covers. It uses the Big-O card's log n reasoning, and it is the lighter sibling of the segment tree on the next card.
expect: low(i) = i & −i, the lowest set bit
t[i] covers the low(i) elements ending at i
query walks down by clearing bits; update walks up by adding them
range sum as a difference of two prefixes
prime.goal: Build a Fenwick tree, trace query and update by hand from the binary of the index, and say which operations it can and can't support.

attend: Why does i & −i isolate the lowest set bit?
Why does a prefix 1..i split into exactly one block per 1-bit of i?
Why does an update climb by adding the lowest bit while a query descends by subtracting it?
Why does a range sum need an inverse operation, and what does that rule out?
How does the 2-D version combine two 1-D walks?

must: t[i] stores the sum of the low(i) elements ending at i → a prefix 1..i is covered by one block per 1-bit of i → query adds t[i] and clears the lowest bit until 0 → at most ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 reads
Element i lies inside exactly the blocks reached by i → i + low(i) → … → each step at least doubles the lowest bit → update touches at most ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 cells (20 at n = 10⁶)
Blocks only give prefixes → a range l..r is query(r) − query(l − 1) → this needs subtraction to undo → works for + and XOR, not for min or max
2-D: t[i][j] covers low(i) rows × low(j) columns → nest the row walk and the column walk → O(log m · log n) per operation, and a rectangle is four prefix rectangles by inclusion–exclusion
elevated: 1-indexing is required → index 0 has no set bit, so i & −i would be 0 and the walks would never move → t[0] is left unused
reference: two's complement as the reason −i flips the bits above the lowest set bit
building by n adds (O(n log n)) versus an O(n) build
the source's C++ NumMatrix line by line
order statistics by binary lifting over the tree

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the 8 bars of t[1..8] for a = [3, 2, −1, 6, 5, 4, −3, 3] (which cells each covers), then write the two loops and one sentence on why each is O(log n).
checklist: odd i covers 1 cell; t[2], t[6] cover 2; t[4] covers 4; t[8] covers all 8
query: s += t[i]; i −= i & −i until 0
update: t[i] += δ; i += i & −i until i > n
one step per 1-bit (query); lowest bit doubles each step (update)
range sums need subtraction, so no min or max

retrieve.q: Explain why a Fenwick tree can answer range sums but not range minimums, even though both are O(log n) in a segment tree.
answer: Fenwick stores prefix blocks only
a range l..r comes from query(r) − query(l − 1), which needs an inverse
min has no inverse: knowing min(1..r) and min(1..l−1) doesn't give min(l..r)
a segment tree stores arbitrary ranges, so it combines without subtracting

retrieve.q: Walk through query(7) after add(3, +2) on the card's array, giving the index sequence and the cells read.
answer: 7 = 0111: read t[7] = −3, clear bit → 6
6 = 0110: read t[6] = 9, clear bit → 4
4 = 0100: read t[4] = 12 (was 10 before the update), clear bit → 0

retrieve.q: Your data never changes after loading and you need 10⁶ range sums. Fenwick, segment tree or prefix-sum array? What does each cost?
answer: prefix-sum array: O(n) build, O(1) per query, the clear winner without updates
Fenwick: O(log n) per query, pointless extra work here
segment tree: O(log n) and 2n to 4n cells
switch to Fenwick the moment point updates appear

compare.q: Fenwick vs segment tree for range sums with point updates: what does each store, what does each support beyond sums, and what does each cost in memory and code?
answer: Fenwick stores prefix blocks sized by the lowest bit; the segment tree stores every half, quarter, eighth
both O(log n) per query and update
the segment tree also does min, max, gcd and lazy range updates
Fenwick: n + 1 ints and about 15 lines; segment tree: 2n to 4n cells and more code

compare.q: A static prefix-sum array vs a Fenwick tree: what does each precompute, and what single requirement decides between them?
answer: prefix sums store every P[i]; any change shifts all later prefixes
Fenwick stores overlapping partial sums so a change touches O(log n) cells
no updates: prefix sums (O(1) queries)
updates interleaved with queries: Fenwick

predict.q: For n = 16, how many cells does add(1, δ) touch, and how many does query(15) read? Which is the worst case for each operation, and why?
predict.answer: add(1) touches 5 cells: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16, the maximum ⌊log₂ 16⌋ + 1, because index 1's lowest bit is as small as possible and must double four times. query(15) reads 4 cells: 15 → 14 → 12 → 8, one per 1-bit of 1111₂; that is the worst query for n = 16 (16 itself is a single read).

apply.task: On the card's array after add(3, +2), compute by hand: query(7), range_sum(2, 7), the cells touched by add(5, δ), the cells touched by add(1, δ), and 12 & −12. Then check with the Fenwick class.
apply.hint: 12 = 1100₂, so its lowest set bit is 100₂.
